item.title: Trump's new spy chief Jay Clayton confirmed by US Senate
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0rd1kl1825o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump's new spy chief Jay Clayton confirmed by US Senate - Published Jay Clayton has been confirmed as the next US director of national intelligence (DNI), after President Donald Trump's original choice was rejected by lawmakers. On Tuesday, the US Senate voted 51 to 47 to install Clayton, replacing the acting DNI Bill Pulte. Pulte was Trump's original pick but faced backlash for being a housing official with no national intelligence experience. Clayton had been serving as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan president Nicholas Maduro. "Jay is outstanding in every way, and will do a spectacular job as Director!" Trump posted afterwards on Truth Social. Clayton, who is also a former securities regulator and federal prosecutor, succeeds Tulsi Gabbard, who left her job last month and was replaced temporarily by Pulte. Pulte's initial appointment in early June raised alarm for both parties, as the Trump loyalist used his other role as federal housing regulator to refer several of the president's political opponents for possible prosecution and oversaw staffing cuts. Shortly before the vote for Clayton's appointment passed, Pulte posted about the cuts on X, writing that "we are, this morning, executing a 5th and near final round of terminations, an approximately 30% staff reduction from weeks ago". Shortly after the alarm in June over Pulte, Trump announced Clayton as his replacement nominee. Senators sought to move quickly with his confirmation. However Clayton's first scheduled appearance before the Senate intelligence committee on 17 June was called off by Trump, who blamed lawmakers for allowing the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa) to lapse. Initially, Democrats welcomed Clayton as a more conventional nominee than Pulte, though their opinion seemed to change during his confirmation hearing earlier this month. Clayton was repeatedly asked whether former Democratic president Joe Biden won the 2020 election, to which he replied by saying that Biden had been "certified" as the winner. "I'm not an election denier," Clayton told senators. Senate Intelligence Committee Vice-Chair Mark Warner, a Democrat, said afterwards that he "came away from [Clayton's] confirmation hearing with serious reservations about whether he would be willing to stand up to political pressure". "I sincerely hope he proves those concerns unfounded, because the Intelligence Community deserves steadier leadership than it has received in recent months," Warner said in his statement. Clayton's confirmation could help revive congressional negotiations on Section 702 of Fisa. This legislation allows the US government to collect communications involving foreigners abroad without an individual warrant, and Trump has been pushing for its long-term renewal. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican, said on Monday: "I hope [Clayton's appointment] will encourage my colleagues to stop blocking reauthorisation of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act". item.title: Trump administration bans new Chinese humanoid robots
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp9e2ex3ekyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump administration bans new Chinese humanoid robots - Published The Trump administration on Tuesday announced a ban on new foreign-made humanoid robot imports to the US over "unacceptable risks" to America's national security. The move applies to advanced robots - including humanoid and four-legged machines. Many of them are made in China, which is competing with the US to develop robotics and artificial intelligence (AI). The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) also banned imports of power inverters - devices used in data centres and solar panels - which it said could also pose a risk to the US economy. The Chinese embassy in Washington said Beijing has long opposed the US' "politicising" of trade issues and sanctions based on "groundless pretexts". FCC chairman Brendan Carr said the agency was doing its part "to secure America's critical supply chains". The FCC has added the items to its Covered List - a register of goods and services that are deemed a risk to US national security. The ban applies to new foreign-produced advanced robotic devices and power inverters and does not prevent the sale or import of any existing models that had been previously authorised by the FCC. The FCC cited concerns that the use of foreign-made inverters could allow overseas firms to turn them off, steal data, facilitate remote access and surveillance by "foreign government actors, or be otherwise exploited through a cyberattack". It added that the use of robots made outside the US could allow "malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots". The Chinese embassy in Washington also said Beijing will "take all necessary measures" in response to any moves that harm its interests, urging all countries to work together to develop AI "for the positive and for good". It called on the US to "abandon its hegemonic mindset, and stop smearing Chinese companies and threatening them with sanctions". The BBC has contacted major Chinese robot manufacturers Unitree, UBTech and AgiBot for comment. - Could humanoid robots be heading for the battlefield? - Published9 June
- Robots available for rent: But what can they do? - Published7 July
China's exports have come under intense scrutiny by the US as the Trump administration attempts to address trade imbalances with the world's second largest economy. Despite being the world's biggest exporter of electric vehicles, China has been effectively shut out of the American market by a steep tariff. Washington has also blocked the sale of cutting-edge US semiconductors to China in a bid to protect national security, slow Beijing's military modernisation and maintain America's lead in AI. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also warned that Chinese AI firms could face sanctions over allegations that they have stolen American intellectual property. In response the Chinese government has said its country's development of AI was "the result of its own dedication and effort as well as international cooperation". The US will be keen to avoid a repeat of the squeeze on supply chains that was triggered last year when China tightened export controls on rare earths - critical for electronics. Chinese technology firms have rapidly developed humanoid robots to be used in settings including factories and homes. Companies have also been quick to market their machines to businesses and the public ahead of US humanoid robot rivals like Elon Musk's Tesla and Boston Dynamics.

item.title: How Mexican drug cartels have outsourced meth labs to Nigeria
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crmrnxp4nllo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How Mexican drug cartels have outsourced meth labs to Nigeria - Published The Nigerian judge was formally dressed, the lawyers maintained legal decorum and protocol was followed – but this hearing was not in the comfortable confines of a Lagos courtroom, it was inside an alleged illicit drug laboratory in the thick of a dense forest. Three Mexicans and seven Nigerians were paraded in handcuffs, as Justice Musa Kakaki inspected the chemicals and equipment they were accused of using to produce the harmful illegal synthetic drug, methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, crystal meth or, locally, ice. A bitter, pungent smell filled the air of the makeshift laboratory, thanks to a large drum of the liquid form of the drug that was crystallising. Another potent odour came from open vats of a dark, viscous liquid, described as "crude", or unprocessed, methamphetamine. Other products were scattered around, including propane gas cylinders and bags of caustic soda, in the unfinished building. This temporary move of the federal high court to a location a two-hour drive from Lagos was an unusual step for Nigeria's judicial system, but the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said it was necessary to understand the scale of the operation. When the suspects were arrested in May, the agency described it as the country's largest-ever meth bust. It said it discovered more than two tonnes of the drug worth some $360m (£270m). The NDLEA at the time announced it had "dealt another crippling blow" and dismantled "a highly sophisticated, multi-million-dollar Nigerian-Mexican methamphetamine production syndicate". The following month, agents found another meth laboratory hidden in a forest in neighbouring Oyo State. That time they arrested five suspects, including one Mexican "methamphetamine expert". The raids underline a broader trend of Africa's, and particularly West Africa's, growing role in the global synthetic drugs trade and the shift by criminal cartels to use the continent, not just as a trafficking hub, but also as a production base. Mexican specialists in manufacturing methamphetamine, often described as "cooks", are increasingly being found working alongside locals in laboratories in Europe and Africa, according to law-enforcement agencies. Meth production has become increasingly sophisticated over the last few decades. "They perfected it, to the point now it is the highest purity, the highest potency version of meth," James Griego, who leads counter-narcotics operations for US-Africa Command (Africom), told the BBC. Africom, which oversees US military operations on the continent, has provided several national anti-drug organisations with intelligence to assist with their raids. "Anybody who is looking to consume methamphetamine, understands that the Mexican meth is the best in the world, for that purpose," Griego added. The first time the NDLEA announced it had discovered a Mexican-linked methamphetamine lab was in 2016, when it described it as a "super lab". These laboratories, where Mexicans have been working, have since been uncovered in Kenya, Mozambique and in South Africa. Since 2023 "we've seen…14 Mexican-operated labs in total [being raided]. We saw the one in 2023 [in Mozambique], we saw six more in 2024, we saw two in 2025 and we've seen five this year," Griego said. "This last year when I talk about the five labs, four of the five are in Nigeria," he added. Intelligence from Africom and the US Drug Enforcement Administration have linked some of the laboratories to Mexico's two biggest drug cartels: the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. Giving testimony to the US Congress in May, Africom commander Gen Dagvin Anderson alleged that militant groups and narco-traffickers have been working together. "African-based terror groups are financed to an increasing degree by drug cartels, expanding those terror groups' reach and lethality," he told lawmakers. Unlike plant-based drugs, such as cocaine or heroin, which can only be grown and processed in certain places, a synthetic drug like meth can be produced anywhere with the right chemicals and expertise, making it easier for organised crime groups to quickly scale up production. Known for its fast and long-lasting effects, methamphetamine delivers a euphoric high, but deeply unpleasant side effects. There is a serious risk of cardiovascular problems, malnourishment through poor diet and, if injecting, blood-borne diseases. Withdrawal from the drug is also very hard as it often includes feelings of anxiety, severe depression, fatigue and intense cravings. As methamphetamine traffickers establish new distribution networks, beyond its historical routes, more people are being exposed to the drug. West Africa poses numerous attractive benefits to Mexican syndicates, starting with swathes of forested land which makes well for secluded production sites. "The population is also an attraction for them, especially the huge youth population because with that you get cheap labour and a market for local consumption," NDLEA spokesperson Femi Babafemi told the BBC. There are fears among authorities that methamphetamine consumption will grow in Nigeria, where a 2018 survey found that 14.4% of the adult population had used an illicit drug - more than twice the global average as estimated by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC). The use of the drug has spread across the continent, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. In East Africa, it has become widely available in countries like Kenya and Tanzania, and also in southern Africa, like in South Africa where it is known as "tik". Drug syndicates are as interested in international drug markets, as they are in the growing local market, and Africa's location makes it easier to reach Asia and Europe. Producing drugs in West Africa gives traffickers access to Atlantic shipping routes. Combined with the region's porous borders and weaker regulation of chemical imports, this helps them cut costs to lucrative consumer markets. In Europe, the UNODC reported a 47% increase in methamphetamine use between 2014 and 2024. In east and south-east Asia seizures of the drug by authorities reached a record high in 2024. "It's a shortening [of] their [supply] line into Asia and a shortening of their pathway into Europe," said Griego. Since returning to office in 2025, US President Donald Trump has intensified efforts against Latin American drug cartels and their operations. "These cartels are feeling the pressure from other parts of the world," said Babafemi, "and so [they] are looking at West Africa as a corporate production hub." Some experts believe tighter scrutiny of traditional trafficking routes from Latin America may be one factor driving cartels to diversify their operations. "That has at least been a part of the calculus of why Mexican cartels have escalated their operations in Africa. That to say though, it is only part of the story," said Griego. "Sinaloa and New Jalisco have always been global organisations. They have operated [in Africa] since the 1990s." But a recent rise in the number of raids on illicit methamphetamine laboratories in Africa could indicate that the cartels are becoming more entrenched on the continent. What is clear is that the trade is no longer just transiting through the continent but finding new manufacturing sites and markets. With measures such as the court hearing at the laboratory, increased surveillance and intelligence use, the Nigerian authorities are adamant they can rise to the challenge. "It's definitely a concern but it helps us stay vigilant and be proactive. This is why we are able to get them before they're able to move out into our communities and into the international market," NDLEA spokesperson Babafemi said. item.title: 'I thought I would die': Survivors describe shock and horror of powerful Japan earthquake
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgw52l5kyyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'I thought I would die': Survivors describe shock and horror of powerful Japan earthquake - Published Business was winding down for the day at Sendan Shokudo, a diner in Japan's south-western city of Yatsushiro, when the whole building suddenly lurched. Everything on the kitchen shelves cascaded to the floor; bowls and glasses shattered. The restaurant's co-owner, 75-year-old Hiroko Ogata, had just walked in. "I was surprised, and scared," she told BBC News. "I went under one of the tables right away, but the table moved sharply towards the right, left, right, left, with me." There's a reason Ogata knew how to react so swiftly: she has lived in Yatsushiro, in central Kumamoto prefecture, her whole life. The area is located on an active tectonic fault system and is no stranger to tremors. In 2016, a pair of earthquakes killed 277 people and injured 2,800 others. But Ogata has "never experienced this big of a jolt". "The last quake 10 years ago was nothing like this one," she said. "I thought I would die." At least 13 people have been killed in the wake of the 6.8-magnitude earthquake that hit Kumamoto late on Tuesday. Of that number, three died in the Aeon shopping mall in Kumamoto city, where a number of people remain unaccounted for. Rescue efforts are under way, but Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has warned that emergency services are in a "race against time". 'Big jolts came one after another' Just a few hundred metres away from the Aeon mall, Yui - who preferred not to use her real name for this report - was sitting in the back office of her cake shop when the quake hit. "I couldn't tell which was the sound of the earthquake and which was the sound of the explosion," she told the BBC. "All I could do was hold the chair I was sitting in as big jolts came one after another," she added, appearing to still be in shock. "I didn't know what to feel; I couldn't even feel scared in such a situation. Even now I don't know what to feel, and I don't know how to explain." Authorities and emergency responders mobilised quickly. Shortly after the tremor struck, Takaichi put 4,600 personnel on the ground to assist with recovery, and said that teams would work "tirelessly through the night" to assess and monitor the damage in affected areas. Tens of thousands of people have experienced power and water outages across Kumamoto City and at least 45 medical facilities have been damaged. The exterior walls of the 17th century Kumamoto Castle, in the city's centre, came toppling down in a plume of dust. The worship hall of the 19th Century Yatshushiro Shrine completely collapsed. One local resident Michal Posan said there is "no water or food left in the stores". Posan, 25, has been living in Kumamoto for two years, and was at home at the time of the quake. "My TV fell on me, my mirror smashed and the roads around me were damaged," she told the BBC – adding that she had started preparing evacuation bags amid the "constant aftershocks". Another resident said aftershocks were still rattling the city hours after the initial tremor. "People are wary of another earthquake on the way," he said. "The 2016 earthquake [was] followed by a second days later." Experts are also concerned. Shinji Kiyomoto of Japan's Meteorological Agency has asked the public to "remain vigilant" for further earthquakes. He too referenced 2016's deadly series of earthquakes, which struck days apart. "We cannot rule out the possibility that an even larger quake could follow this time as well," he said. "We urge people to remain on alert." Kyushu island, where Kumamoto prefecture is located, is a spiderweb of active fault zones. These include the Hinagu fault, which runs about 81km through the island's heartland. That fault zone was partially activated in the 2016 quakes – but experts have long warned that its remaining, unruptured sections could generate a major earthquake. Assessments by the government's earthquake research committee suggest that tremors with magnitudes as high as 7.5 could strike along the inland section of the zone. If the whole Hinagu fault were to rupture, the magnitude could reach 8. In the meantime, locals like Ogata and Yui are having to pick up the pieces and try to restore some kind of normality – even as the shockwaves, both geological and psychological, continue to occur. "The whole of my place is messy, and I don't know where to stand – but we have to earn our living by restarting our restaurant as soon as possible, so I am cleaning the place today," Ogata said on Wednesday. "But when I try to work for a bit, an aftershock occurs and I have to stop – then I do some work and we have another aftershock… So it is going so slowly. "If we keep having this many aftershocks it will be very stressful." Yui's cake shop remains closed, as she assesses the extent of the damage. "I haven't checked whether the machines such as the oven are working," she said. "After I check those, I will have an idea whether I can go back to business or not."

item.title: 'Israeli settlers laid siege to our home': Inside a Palestinian village under weekly attack
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyxgn37lg5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'Israeli settlers laid siege to our home': Inside a Palestinian village under weekly attack - Published The large, bolted gate of the Abu Alia family compound in al-Mughayyir village held firm against the teenage settlers; its thin metal bars ringing with each blow, as they smashed it again and again with their clubs. But the insults hurled by both sides that day passed freely through the bars. One offensive slur - almost identical in both Hebrew and Arabic - delivered with nonchalant contempt by the Israeli boys bashing at the gate; and with fear and frustration by the Palestinian man inches away from them on the other side, filming the encounter on his phone. This gate, on the edge of al-Mughayyir, has become a weekly frontline in the battle for the occupied West Bank. And this kind of attack by settlers on Palestinian homes, a weekly routine in villages across the territory. When we arrived in al-Mughayyir that day, the confrontation at the Abu Alia compound had already begun. The Israeli army and border police were already moving through the streets, and residents were running from their vehicles - soldiers, like settlers, are seen as the enemy here. Some young men rolled rocks into the road to block it, as the sound of gunshots cracked over the village. On the hill above them, the local mosque was calling on people to help the family trapped by the settlers. But slipping past Israeli soldiers has become a dangerous gamble. Residents, medical workers and journalists have all been shot during Israeli military operations in the West Bank. This is what passes for a normal weekend now in al-Mughayyir, and in villages across the West Bank, but it rarely breaks beyond the local news. We spent a week around al-Mughayyir, and its neighbouring village, Khirbet Abu Falah, to see what life was like here for a single community, or a single family. What we found shows how quickly control of this landscape is changing, and how local attacks by settlers here are the tip of a national project to bring West Bank land under Israeli control. Since occupying the West Bank during the 1967 Middle East war, Israel has built more than 100 settlements housing more than half a million Jews on land Palestinians want for a future state. Some Israeli settlers have also established hundreds of wildcat outposts - often starting with a single tent or caravan on a hilltop, and often very close to Palestinian homes. Both Israel's official settlements and its outposts are illegal under international law. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has described those carrying out settler attacks as a handful of misguided young people: "150 juvenile delinquents", he's called them, or "70 teenagers from broken homes". The settlers smashing the Abu Alia gate that Saturday in al-Mughayyir seemed to be mainly teenagers, but earlier that day, a settler group had put out a call on social media to "expel the enemy", including a quote from the Torah. "If you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land from before you, those you leave will become spikes in your eyes and thorns in your sides," it says. And behind the young faces at the gate in al-Mughayyir were much older settlers - at least one of them armed - standing with Israeli soldiers not far from the house. There is a widespread belief among Palestinians in the West Bank that Israeli soldiers support settlers during these attacks. Footage of the confrontation at the gate, filmed by the Abu Alia family, shows soldiers strolling up to the teenagers who are attacking it, and making gentle moves to guide them away. It is not effective: the teenagers return again and again to smash their clubs against the gate, as a woman inside screams at them to get away. The soldiers standing with them at the gate make no attempt to question or detain the attackers, or even confiscate their clubs. Footage, also filmed from the Abu Alia compound, appears to show young settlers breaking fencing around the property, as soldiers stand by a short distance away, helmets off, phones out. In one photo, there appears to be an angle-grinder or similar power tool lying on a log behind them. We later photographed it in the hands of soldiers, then in the hands of settlers, then with soldiers again at the Abu Alias' fence. We asked the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) about these incidents. It gave no explanation for the events, but said in a general response that it was investigating claims of damage to property. Rafeeq Abu Alia, who was one of the family members in the house that day, told me the attack had followed a familiar pattern. "First thing this morning, they came... There were four settlers and they were armed. Then more settlers came and laid siege to the house, insulting and provoking us," he said. "They came with the army. The soldiers entered, followed by the settlers. The army beat people inside the house." We filmed soldiers trying to break down the Abu Alias' gate that day, while settlers stood beside them. And later saw workers fixing the broken entrance. Medics told us they had treated several Palestinians for tear gas and beating injuries, and that another person had been taken to hospital with a gunshot wound. The IDF told us its forces had been in al-Mughayyir that day, responding to reports of a confrontation between Palestinians and Israeli civilians. It said soldiers had entered a house in the village to search for suspects throwing stones, and separately, that they had detained one person taking part in what it called a "violent riot". It said it was investigating allegations of violence by soldiers. It also said masked Palestinians had used slings to hurl stones at soldiers, that its forces fired to remove the threat, and that "a hit was identified", meaning someone was shot. The rules of engagement for Israeli forces in the West Bank were loosened to allow soldiers to use live fire against Palestinians throwing stones, after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 that triggered the Gaza war. Our repeated requests to film with the IDF on patrol in the West Bank this year have so far gone unanswered. As Israeli forces fired live rounds, stun grenades and tear-gas canisters into al-Mughayyir that day, we walked down a largely empty road towards the Abu Alia compound, to see the situation first-hand. Two soldiers appeared in front of us, metres away. Our local Palestinian producer was the first to notice them. We were still filming as one raised his weapon, pointing towards us. We headed up to a nearby roof for safety - the army vehicle and soldiers visible right below us. Within seconds of our arrival, they motioned for us to stop filming. One raised a tear-gas launcher towards us. We moved back from the edge of the roof. He never fired. Access to stories like this is getting harder here, even for journalists with official Israeli government accreditation. Palestinian paramedics say they are also routinely blocked. An ambulance worker with the Palestinian Red Crescent told me that while he was responding to a call from al-Mughayyir that week during another settler attack, Israeli soldiers took the keys to his ambulance, after telling him to turn off the engine. "If they tell us to stay there, we have to stay and wait, regardless of the situation," he said. "It's something we face all the time." Al-Mughayyir is an isolated village, surrounded by areas which were temporarily left under full Israeli control during the Oslo peace process 30 years ago. That peace process later collapsed. In the past few years, Israeli settlement outposts - illegal under both Israeli and international law - have mushroomed around it. A member of the village council, a man known as Abu Waheed, told me that settlers came into al-Mughayyir every day, and that when the settlers told soldiers to do something, the soldiers did it. "[They come] with the army, and with the cars of the army," he said. "Here and here and here. The army is the settlers, but their clothes are green." Many Israeli soldiers serving here are settlers themselves and see the West Bank as land given to them by God. Thousands of settlers were also directly recruited into local security squads here after the 7 October Hamas attacks, and given weapons, with minimal vetting or training. Army figures say most of those squads have now been disbanded, following multiple reports of abuse against Palestinian residents. None of the outposts we approached around al-Mughayyir responded to our request for an interview. But one settler in a nearby outpost recently spoke to an Israeli documentary team about his work in a security squad. "We are the residents, and we are carrying out a conquest here," Adar Lafair told the Kan 11 documentary team. "We're settling on land that years ago we couldn't have walked on. We wouldn't have dared to walk on. Arabs controlled this area. But today, we're here." His wife Rivka said she dreamed of the squads being allowed to "conquer" a nearby Palestinian village. Describing the creation of her outpost by Israeli settlers, she said control of the area was taken by "a group of 17-year-old kids with no weapons, with nothing". "They simply got into fights over the land. They just showed who was in charge. And we're the ones in charge of this land," she said. "It shouldn't be that teenagers go up onto a hilltop and safeguard the security of the entire people of Israel by doing that. It should be the army that clears the way." One Israeli soldier who served in the West Bank recently told me that extremist settlers saw him as the enemy for not supporting their attacks. He asked us to hide his identity. "There are teenagers there who look at you with hate," he said. "There was one who told us, 'I will put a bullet in your head.'" He said it was clear that the attacks were not the work of just a few radical teenagers. "There are bodies that equip them with this ideology, with food and water, and logistical support, and also guidance on how to do this." Asked about claims by some settlers that Palestinian attacks on them go unreported, he said that claim did not match the reality he had seen on the ground. "In the Palestinian faces, I saw only fear," he said. "I never saw any fear on any Jew that lived there. They feel there is no law. They feel that they can attack in the middle of the day, and nothing will happen." In the week we were there, the UN counted 45 Palestinians injured by Israeli settlers in attacks across the West Bank, including 12 children. It says injuries linked to settler attacks have risen sharply, to more than three per day since the start of this year. Settler attacks have risen as the number of settler outposts has grown. These outposts are officially illegal under Israeli law, but that has not stopped Israel supporting them with roads and electricity, or legalising dozens of them after they appear. The Israeli organisation Peace Now, which monitors settlements, says at least 231 new outposts have so far been created under this Israeli government. Some, used as settler shepherding farms, now effectively control 18% of the West Bank, it says, driving out more than 100 Palestinian communities. At a conference of settler leaders in July, the IDF commander for the West Bank, Maj Gen Avi Bluth, said farm outposts "align well" with Israel's security concept, "provided that this is also reflected in operational conduct, as well as ethical conduct, and in accordance with the law". "All of this greatly strengthens security," he said. Israel's current government has so far provided 19bn shekels ($6.2bn) to expanding settlements in the West Bank, and is now seeking another 600m shekels ($196m) for settlement programmes, according to Peace Now. The government, which includes religious-nationalist settlers among its cabinet ministers, has also lifted a 20-year ban on Israelis settling in areas around the Palestinian city of Jenin in the far north of the territory. It is pushing ahead with construction on more than a dozen settlements there, as well as several new military sites, including one next to the refugee camp in Jenin - the first time Israel has seized land for a military site in an area put under total Palestinian control in the Oslo Accords. Hagit Ofran from Peace Now says the rapid construction in Jenin is part of a wider race by the Israeli government to expand settlements in the West Bank before Israeli elections are held in October. And, she says, Israel is also finding ways to funnel state money to settler outposts that were illegal under Israeli law, via allocations for roads, "security needs" or the establishment of "temporary sites" in new areas earmarked for settlement. In Khirbet Abu Falah, right next door to al-Mughayyir, Brahim Hamayel, an olive farmer I met during a previous settler attack a year ago, told me four new outposts had appeared nearby since then - two of them just in the previous month. He pointed out one of them on a nearby hill - built, he said, on private Palestinian land, in an area that is supposed to be run by the Palestinian Authority. And the attacks had increased too, he said, sometimes targeting the village itself at night. "Since we met last year, the attacks have moved from our farms to our homes," he said. "All my neighbours have been hurt one way or the other; some had their houses or cars burned down. We're putting up barbed wire for protection, as if our houses have become prisons." While we were talking, we saw smoke rising from the village fields. We watched as settlers moved around the smouldering land. An Israeli army jeep quickly arrived, but it did not stop the settlers starting a second fire, or driving straight past them, back towards one of the new outposts Brahim had pointed out. This road past their fields, increasingly overlooked by settler outposts, has become a gauntlet for farmers here, to be run at speed in vehicles without stopping or getting out. It is the only open route between Khirbet Abu Falah and al-Mughayyir. Twice when we drove along it, we saw an Israeli settler sitting in the empty fields. One week after the attack in al-Mughayyir, Palestinian residents were still paying the price. Seventeen-year-old Fadi Hamdallah al-Nassan, shot in the leg that day, had died of his injuries. A football player with the Palestinian national youth team, he was carried back through the village streets for burial. The next day, two more Palestinians were killed in another settler attack nearby. Another routine weekend in the occupied West Bank: roads closed, land taken, villages under siege, families broken. Additional reporting by Rebecca Hartmann - Published4 days ago

item.title: Thousands sheltering in key Sudan city under threat again as fighting escalates
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gx399l0wyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'No safe options' for thousands sheltering in key Sudan city as RSF fighters advance - Published Thousands of people who have poured into the city of el-Obeid hoping to find shelter from Sudan's raging civil war have found themselves under threat again, amid warnings that paramilitary fighters are preparing to descend on the army-controlled city. Clashes between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the military has escalated in the North Kordofan region - a critical target for both sides in the conflict which could open a gateway into contested territory. Displaced people have flocked to el-Obeid, which remains heavily defended by the Sudanese military, despite ongoing strikes being carried out on the city as paramilitary forces advance. The UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) said it has become a key refuge for people escaping ongoing violence in the surrounding areas. Satellite imagery shows the main displacement camp has expanded significantly since March, with aid workers reporting dozens of new arrivals each day. "Families have run out of safe options to protect themselves," Mohamed Refaat, IOM chief of mission in Sudan, said. "Many have already been displaced before and are once again forced to leave behind their homes, livelihoods and support networks." The UN and G7 foreign ministers have now issued warnings that the RSF may be preparing to attack the city, raising fears that atrocities akin to those seen during the massacre in el-Fasher could be repeated. Thousands of people were killed in mass executions after the paramilitary overran SAF troops defending the city last October, in one of the worst atrocities since the civil war began in 2023. Fears of similar reprisals occurring in el-Obeid have grown for weeks and verified footage now shows dozens of heavily armed RSF troops in armoured trucks stationed in Nyala, a key nearby stronghold, vowing to "liberate" the city. The RSF launched a record number of drone strikes on the city in June, according to the monitoring group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (Acled). The number of attacks only fell in July because the RSF was responding to Sudanese military attacks elsewhere in Sudan, analysts added. Satellite images show that despite the strikes, el-Obeid's displacement camp has continued to swell, with hundreds of new tents erected since March. The UN has estimated that more than 83,000 civilians have now fled fighting in other parts of the state and sought shelter in the city. As the displacement camps have expanded, the conditions in el-Obeid have deteriorated. Last week the UN warned nearly 400,000 people in the city's vicinity are facing food shortages, following a sustained effort by RSF commanders to cut off supply routes into the city for months, creating what one UN official called a "functional siege". Locals have previously said that supply convoys attempting to reach the city have been targeted by drone attacks, while the charity Islamic Relief - which has operated aid stations in el-Obeid - told BBC Verify that flights carrying aid arriving via the airport have also stopped. Aid agencies say the food and water shortages have been exacerbated by RSF drone strikes on critical infrastructure. Verified video footage last month showed a massive explosion at a fuel station in the heart of the city after one such strike, while satellite images also appear to damage to power stations and supply warehouses in the city's market district. One humanitarian official working with Islamic Relief said the slowing of drone strikes in recent days has improved the situation in the city. But he emphasised that while more aid is being distributed and some power has been restored, the situation remained extremely "unpredictable" - with fuel shortages still an issue. "Every day we are seeing new arrivals due to fighting in areas around El-Obeid. It is not possible to get the exact number of people who are arriving on a daily basis, but it would be about 80 or 100 households daily," the aid worker said. Meanwhile, RSF fighters and leaders have repeatedly vowed in verified video footage to move on the city. In one clip posted to the paramilitary's official Telegram channel, a commander could be seen waving an assault rifle while addressing a group of troops - promising that they would soon see combat in el-Obeid. Another verified clip from late May showed paramilitary fighters gathering alongside dozens of armoured vehicles just outside the RSF heartland of Nyala. One fighter seen leaning on the door of an armoured vehicle boasted that the unit's next target was el-Obeid. Recent footage located by BBC Verify placed fighters within 40km (24 miles) of the city. These threats also appear to be stoking tensions within the city. Volker Türk, the UN's High Commissioner for Human Rights, recently said that many displaced people who have sought shelter in el-Obeid have faced suspicion and hostility from locals over fears that RSF sympathisers are infiltrating the city. Meanwhile, the Sudanese military appears to be digging in and building a defensive berm - or earth wall - around the city, satellite images suggest. Unlike the one built around el-Fasher by the RSF last year, which trapped people inside the besieged city, this appears to be defensive and aimed at keeping attackers out. On Monday, the military also said that a massive operation had secured a vital highway between el-Obeid and the capital, Khartoum. In response, the RSF's leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, who is known as Hemedti, said he was "unleashing" his fighters and ordered his front-line commanders to "move straight forward. No more retreat. No more hesitation". Nohad Eltayeb, Senior Research Assistant at Acled, told BBC Verify that the city is a key hub for both sides to the conflict. "It is the critical juncture connecting RSF-controlled western territories with the military-held central and White Nile regions," Eltayeb said. She added that the RSF "need to regain momentum following territorial losses in the eastern Blue Nile region, alongside internal instability and defections within its Darfur strongholds". The joint EU/G7 warning of atrocities in el-Obeid urged all "external actors" to suspend "armed, logistical, or financial support to the parties to the conflict". Earlier this month the European Parliament expressly named the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as a key backer of the RSF. Emirati officials have repeatedly denied the allegations. Alan Boswell, Crisis Group's Horn of Africa Group director, suggested that the flurry of early Western interventions may be motivated by the failure to avert the el-Fasher massacre - which was the culmination of an extended siege and RSF build-up. "Many are trying to turn up the volume on those warnings to prevent another round of mass atrocities in el-Obeid," he said. "The key is if world leaders will put enough pressure on the RSF and its main backer to make a difference this time." - Published25 February

item.title: Why Wimbledon is serving Indian ice cream and Bollywood beats
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckgdz0420xzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Why Wimbledon is serving Indian ice cream and Bollywood beats - Published Few things are more sacrosanct in sport than Wimbledon. Its all-white dress code for players, minimalist court-side advertising and association with strawberries and cream all remain fiercely guarded traditions. Yet as the organisers of the world's oldest Grand Slam set out to crack cricket-obsessed India this year, Wimbledon had to abandon some of its trademark restraint to win over audiences in a country where tennis remains a niche sport. Strawberries and cream got an Indian makeover after Wimbledon partnered with a historic Delhi kulfi (Indian ice cream) maker. Its Instagram channel shared reels of Roger Federer and other stars gliding across the court to popular 1990s Bollywood hits. The championships also welcomed celebrity cricketers and Indian influencers to the Royal Box, using their star power to broaden its appeal. Wimbledon also hyper-localised its marketing effort with digital content scattered across various Indian languages. The effort seems to have paid off. Jannik Sinner's win over Alexander Zverev in the men's final reportedly drew some 2.7 million livestream viewers, external despite being played after midnight local time. And on average 8,53,000 viewers tuned in to watch the tournament in India this year - up 18% over last - according to local media. JioStar - the platform which holds exclusive streaming rights for the matches - declined to share official data with the BBC. Wimbledon's push to win India is strategic and not accidental, Darshana Bhalla, a sports branding expert told the BBC. India is already Wimbledon's largest international audience by reach, and 2026 is a particularly important year with Arnav Paparkar becoming the first Indian in 36 years to reach the under-18 boys singles quarter finals. "India is also seeing a stronger pipeline of young talent across both ATP and ITF circuits than it has in nearly a decade, and premium urban sports consumption is expanding rapidly beyond cricket, with streaming platforms able to target niche audiences at scale," says Bhalla. The organisers of the game are capitalising on these shifts. Sally Bolton, chief executive of the All England Lawn Tennis Club, Wimbledon's governing body, earlier told the Financial Times, external, that India has joined the US as a "main focus" for growing the grand slam's audience. But with the country likely to become the world's most important growth market for sport in the coming years - the sector is estimated to grow at a compounded 12-14% rate to 2030, nearly double the global average according to KPMG, external - tournaments like Wimbledon are having to be more culturally specific in the way they engage Indian audiences. "Wimbledon has understood one of the biggest shifts in global marketing. For decades, premium brands believed exclusivity came from distance. However, today they understand that exclusivity comes from belonging," says Bhalla. "What they've changed is the entry point, instead of asking young Indians to first understand Wimbledon...they are allowing Indians to discover Wimbledon through familiar cultural cues. Like the kulfi collaboration, Punjabi, Bollywood and Tamil music infusion and Indian creators." This, she says, is not just tactical social media engagement, but the creation of a cultural bridge for a vast potential audience currently focused on cricket. For many younger Indians to whom Wimbledon can feel aspirational but also distant, "reducing this cultural distance" is important, Upasna Dash, founder of the Jajabor Brand Consultancy, told the BBC. Its focus on social media led marketing is also rooted in how people discover events these days, she adds. "Younger audiences often encounter global events through social media before they engage with the event itself. Instead of asking consumers to enter Wimbledon's world, the campaign briefly enters theirs." For streaming platforms like JioStar too, the tournament offers a chance to broaden engagement with a new demographic, create calendar events and move away from focusing on a single sport. It has been widely reported that JioStar was seeking to renegotiate, external its $3bn broadcast rights contract with the International Cricket Council for 2024-2027 due to financial losses. The partnership still remains in force, but in such a scenario of uncertainty, increasing investment in tennis makes strategic sense, say experts. "For JioStar, tennis broadens the engagement calendar, attracts affluent urban audiences and diversifies advertiser categories beyond cricket," says Bhalla. "In India, cricket gives scale, tennis gives premium audiences…Wimbledon brings something cricket cannot - a premium, affluent, English-speaking, urban audience that brands in luxury, automotive, banking, fintech, travel and premium consumer goods actively." Yet, for all the awareness the branding blitz has created around the tournament to convert to sustained, long term engagement with the sport, Wimbledon will have to "create lasting relevance long after the tournament ends", according to Aryan Anurag, co-founder, Binge Labs, a Delhi-based social media agency. "If [these moments] are treated as one-off campaign tactics around a tournament, the impact is likely to be short-lived." For the curiosity to translate into genuine fandom, there will have to be more grassroots engagement and continued market investment, adds Dash. But for now, every major global sports property is watching Wimbledon's experiment, says Bhalla. "If it demonstrates that culturally contextualised storytelling can materially increase engagement in India, then expect F-1, the NBA, the NFL, the UFC, La Liga and the Premier League to deepen their India-first content strategies." item.title: The cocaine superhighway from Ecuador to Europe - the BBC reports on gangs and the police fightback
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdx7n1r54nno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
On the front line of Ecuador's drugs war, police fight gangs, guns and corruption - Published In the Ecuadoran city of Durán, riddled with drugs and rival gangs, Police Captain Jean Carlos Bustamante knows exactly what he is up against – not just the criminals who kill and sometimes dismember their rivals, but also the enemy within. "We have many, many bad people inside our unit, inside the state, inside politics," he says. "We have many, many guys that are corrupt. They are in the pay of the gangs." The only police officers he can trust, he says, are the ones right beside him - members of his hand-picked team. At 34, Captain Bustamante is the oldest among them and moves like the special forces officer he used to be. With the sun setting, he leads his team into a hardscrabble neighbourhood where windows are sealed off behind metal grills, and lips are sealed by fear. This is the heart of gangland, controlled by a group called Los Aguilas (Spanish for The Eagles). I ask what happens if local people speak out against the gangs. "They kill them," the captain replies. "So that's why they never say nothing." He's heading for an abandoned house where he believes weapons have been hidden (gunmen don't keep their guns at home). He and his team line up, hugging the wall, heavily armed, and tightly packed. A battering ram gets them through the door. They find two handguns – one rusty but the other ready to be fired - and ammunition for an assault rifle. The captain says he's happy with the result. "The first reason is because we are safe," he says. "The second is that there are two guns less for the gangs." But this is a small victory, in a war of attrition. He admits the gangs have "many weapons and much more money than the state". He knows the risks only too well – having lost three close friends fighting the gangs. He has also lost his fear he says, "years ago", but his parents have not. "My mum says 'be careful, maybe you can die there'," he tells me. "My dad calls all the time and asks 'my son, are you good? Tell me that you are good.'" A line can be traced - in dollars and in broken lives - from the back streets of Durán to the hotspots of London, and other capital cities. Around 70% of the cocaine reaching Europe and the US is funnelled out of Ecuador, according to the country's President, Daniel Noboa. How did it come to this? The drug pours in from neighbouring Colombia and Peru – the two biggest producers in the world. Powerful home-grown gangs – with links to Mexican cartels and Albanian mafia groups – help smuggle the cocaine onwards. They take advantage of Ecuador's weak border controls, underfunded security forces, and long Pacific coast. In the process what was a peaceful tourist haven in South America has – in under a decade - become a killing ground. Last year the murder rate was one of the highest in the world, with more than 9,200 people killed, according to Ecuador's interior ministry. That's despite an iron-fisted crackdown by President Noboa over the past two years. Critics say it has backfired. Top crime bosses have been arrested, causing the gangs to fracture, but also to multiply. Many here believe the war against the gangs will never be won. Captain Bustamante keeps fighting. When we join him for another operation he's lying in wait getting a bird's eye view of the back alleys from a drone. He sees three figures moving around at the edge of a playground – "micro-traffickers" - caught in the act, he says. They are at the bottom of the drug chain, selling locally, in minute amounts, not kilos. Within minutes he and his team have tracked the suspects to their door. The battering ram is out again, and soon they are in the kitchen, where a middle-aged woman protests, and a young girl bursts into tears. The police move from room to room, by torchlight - there's no power - opening wardrobes and lifting mattresses. Upstairs, they find a hiding place behind a window. A young suspect emerges and is detained. Two others are handcuffed in another room. All three are led away, denying that they were dealing drugs. Nearby the captain finds tiny paper packets of "H" stashed in a flowerpot. It's a highly addictive mix containing small amounts of heroin sold by neighbourhood dealers for $1.00 (£0.75) per packet. One of the suspects is charged, and if convicted, he could get five years in jail. Prosecutors release the other two. Senior officers say that happens a lot. They blame corruption in the justice system, and the prosecutor's office. "We imprison them [gang members] and they release them," says Colonel Santiago Gavilanez, deputy commander of Durán police. "We know because when we carry out raids, we recapture them. Some of those who are released kill people and leave orphans behind." He tells us that the gangs have money to "buy laws, judges, and politicians". We get an example of the buying power of the gangs from another police officer, in a different location. For his safety, we cannot reveal his name or where he is based. He told us he was contacted twice by text and offered a massive bribe - "enough money to retire on". He turned it down. Someone – a colleague perhaps – had informed the gang exactly where he worked and what he did. "You never know who is watching," he said. We heard that a lot during a week in Durán, and surrounding areas. Back at the playground it's the end of another long day in body armour, but Captain Bustamante says he has to keep going. "Maybe, I am a little tired," he admits, "but it's my work. I believe we can win this war. We have to do it." As we speak, one of the main gang bosses in the area has been spotted nearby. "We know he controls the dealers," says the captain, "but we have no leads or evidence, so we can't arrest him". But police here insist they are having an impact. The murder rate in Durán is down by half, they say, in the first six months of this year. There are other indications of progress, they tell us, with streets no longer deserted after 19:00 local time, and bodies no longer found beheaded or dismembered. That used to be common, according to Colonel Gavilanez. "We have managed to contain the gangs," he says. "Getting complete control is going to be a medium-term process." Elsewhere the criminals are containing the police. Through a contact we arranged to meet a local gang on their home turf, about an hour's drive from the city. Their leader – whom we are calling Jonathan – told me he had four officers on his payroll. "Whenever they're going to do an operation, they call me," he said. "They tell me to hide things, and to get out of here. When they arrive, they find nothing." That early warning systems costs him about $1,500 (£1,100) to $2,000 (£1,500) a month. At 37, Jonathan is just a few years older than Captain Bustamante, but he's across enemy lines. He says he joined a gang, at 18, to put food on the table. He and his men (and boys) strolled through the rough-hewn streets, in broad daylight, brandishing weapons - including a semi-automatic rifle and a pistol. The youngest gang member we saw was a lean 17-year-old, wearing a bulletproof vest, and flip flops. All covered their faces. Jonathan answered our questions inside a narrow room in a breeze block house, with his lieutenants crowding in. Most of the space was taken up by a bed. He admitted to being a drug pusher and a killer. "How many lives have you taken?" I asked. "Well, until now about eight, I think. I don't remember well," he replied, with a handgun in his lap, pointing in my direction. Jonathan claimed his gang didn't kill innocent people, just a rival criminal group trying to replace them. "They want to force their way in here," he said, "they come killing people, and we respond. The main thing for us now is to eliminate the other gang." As we spoke, local people gathered near the doorway, children among them. Human rights workers in Ecuador told us boys can be recruited into gang life by the age of 12. Three years later they can be hitmen. Jonathan makes no apologies for putting guns in the hands of teenagers or selling cocaine in the neighbourhood he claims to protect. He insists the drug trade cannot be rooted out. "I think it's an issue that will never end," he says. "If they shut us down, another one [gang] will come along, and if they shut that one down, there will be another." He expects to die, as he has lived – by the gun. "Death is paid by death," he said. "But if they come to kill me, I won't make it easy for them." Two nights later, back in Durán, we saw how gangs settle scores. The body of a man was visible under flashing police lights, lying where he fell, beside a motorbike. Bullet casings were still on the ground. Neighbours stood looking on, mostly in silence. A man and woman held each other and wept – relatives of the dead man. Police suspected a revenge attack – one gang against another. Forensic teams lifted the body onto a stretcher, and into the back of a refrigerated van: violent death, on repeat. Another corpse was already inside. A witness was willing to speak – but not to be named. "He already had a bullet in his back," he told us. "As he fell, they finished him off with a shot to the head. He was shot six times by two men on a motorbike." "We are used to this now because it happens every day," he said. "You might just step outside and catch a stray bullet. You can't even go out or talk to friends or family because someone could shoot you." He does not expect the president's fight against the gangs to deliver any change. "Criminals are like ghosts," he said, in a low voice. "They pop up wherever they please." Then he melted away, into the warm night air. You never know who is watching. With additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant, Chris Gibson, Thalie Ponce and Mauricio Torres.

item.title: European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj638jx0l53o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Devastating European wildfires in maps - and how they're being tackled - Published Since mid-July wildfires have torn through France, Spain, and Portugal forcing more than 300,000 people to evacuate their homes. Officials in the Spanish capital Madrid have said the fires are the worst the region have ever experienced. French President Emmanuel Macron, visiting the fire-ravaged area in the Gironde region, called the "completely unprecedented" wildfire the "toughest since World War Two". The fires have broken out amid a sweltering summer of heatwaves across Europe. Both France and Spain are now seeing another sharp rise in temperatures, with peaks of 41-42C expected in France. Wildfires in the regions outside Madrid have burned about 606 sq miles (1570 sq km) since 1 July, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (Effis). That is an area more than twice as large as the city itself. In France, the worst affected area has been the Gironde, around the city of Bordeaux, where more than 200,000 people were forced from their homes. From 22 July the blaze spread rapidly, tearing through forests and fields in France's famous wine region, and burning more than 162 sq miles (420 sq km) in less than four days - an area roughly four times the size of Paris. At its peak, the wildfire came as close as nine miles (15km) from the south of Bordeaux, although the city was never under serious threat. The fires have also came close to a number of sensitive military and industrial sites in the area, including facilities that work on French ballistic missiles, rocket motors, and the processing of hazardous chemicals. The fires became so extreme they created their own giant fire thunderstorm. A rare weather event, storms like these are formed when heat from the wildfires makes the air above the fire rise rapidly, carrying smoke, ash and water vapour high into the atmosphere. As the air rises, it cools, and the water vapour condenses into a cloud. If the fire is powerful enough and the atmosphere is unstable, that cloud can grow into a cumulonimbus - the same type of cloud associated with thunderstorms. If these clouds then become large enough, they can produce their own lightning, which can then start new fires. They can also occasionally bring hail and rain. These extreme and unpredictable conditions make the fires all the more difficult to stop. To combat them, French firefighters have been using planes loaded with fire retardant, as well as planes like the Canadair, which can scoop 6,000 litres of water from lakes or the sea in 12 seconds and drop it directly on the fires. On dangerous days, loaded aircraft patrol high-risk areas before any fires have been reported, so they can drop within minutes of a sighting. Planes often fly in a continuous shuttle while retardant is laid along the edges of the fire and ground crews attack the flames directly. 1 of 3 In Gironde, about 2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel, and 1,200 police officers and gendarmes have been involved in tackling the blaze. Four French firefighters have died while on duty, officials say. But even with these numbers, Gironde official Jean-Luc Gleyze told the BBC that authorities don't have enough people to combat the fires. "We don't have enough people and enough trucks and even I think France don't have enough," he said. Around the town of Lacanau, bulldozers, diggers and mechanical shovels were used to carve a firebreak that is 100m (328ft) wide at points, according to French media. A firebreak is a stretch of land that has been stripped of all vegetation to stop the fire from spreading - removing any potential fuel before the fire has a chance to reach it. Spanish teams have been using many of the same techniques to tackle their wildfires, which are on course to become the worst the country has seen in two decades. Francisco Martín, a government delegate in Madrid, described one of the fires as "undoubtedly the largest fire in the history of the Madrid region". This summer's fires have been aided by the hotter, drier conditions caused by climate change, which allow fires to spread faster and burn more fiercely. "The climate emergency is worsening year after year, and we are required to be united to fight against fire, as well as in prevention and reconstruction," Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said. Appealing to his country's regional governments, Sánchez added: "Climate denial is the worst fuel for the fight against the climate emergency." 1 of 5 Additional reporting by Elizabeth Rizzini and Helen Willetts. Confronting gang members at the heart of Ecuador's drug battle The BBC's Orla Guerin goes on patrol with Ecuador's police, who are grappling with a huge surge in drug crime. Drugs have been pouring into Ecuador from neighbouring Colombia and Peru - the two biggest producers in the world. Powerful home-grown gangs, with links to Mexican cartels and Albanian mafia groups, are then helping to smuggle the cocaine onwards. Last year, Ecuador's murder rate was one of the highest in the world, with more than 9,200 people killed, according to the country's interior ministry.
